title: Weight loss surgery (metabolic and bariatric surgery) | NHS inform
text:
Weight loss surgery (metabolic and bariatric surgery)
Weight loss surgery is sometimes used to treat people who are living with complex obesity. Its also known as metabolic and bariatric surgery.
Am I eligible for weight loss surgery?
It may be a treatment option for people who:
have a Body Mass Index (BMI) of more than 35 with a weight related condition like
Type 2 diabetes
have been part of a weight and lifestyle management programme
are medically fit for surgery
have been assessed by a bariatric surgical team to consider any additional psychological or dietary needs you may have, as part of your overall medical care
You may not be considered for surgery if you are
actively smoking or using e-cigarettes (vapes)
.
If you want to know more about access to weight loss surgery in your health board, speak to your healthcare professional.
Types of weight loss surgery
The most common procedures offered are a sleeve gastrectomy and gastric bypass. Both these surgeries work by altering signals that are sent from your gut that drive your appetite, hunger and blood sugar levels.
Sleeve gastrectomy
This is commonly known as a gastric sleeve. This involves converting your stomach into a long thin tube or ‘sleeve’. The stomach is stapled along its length in a vertical direction. The surgeon removes about 70% of your stomach during the procedure.
The smaller stomach pouch, or sleeve, will reduce your ability to eat large portions. This should help you feel satisfied for longer with smaller food portions. This is a permanent procedure and cannot be reversed.
Image showing a stomach before and after gastric sleeve surgery
Gastric bypass
A smaller stomach is created which will restrict your food intake. A section (about a 1/3) of your intestine is bypassed.
The bypass surgery helps you lose weight by reducing the amount of calories your body can absorb. This reduces hunger and makes you feel fuller, quicker, meaning you eat less.
This is a permanent procedure and highly unlikely to be reversed.
Fewer vitamins and minerals (especially iron) are absorbed as food passes through the intestine.
Other weight loss surgery options
In some cases other procedures may be considered like a gastric balloon or gastric band. Your healthcare professional will discuss these options with you if appropriate.
Most weight loss surgeries are done using minimally invasive methods (laparoscopy). You’ll also be under a
general anaesthetic
.
Benefits of weight loss surgery
The benefits of weight loss surgery include:
long term weight reduction
remission or improvement of
type 2 diabetes
improved
cholesterol levels
reduced
blood pressure
improved
obstructive sleep apnoea
(disturbed sleep)
less joint pain
better mobility
reduction in medications
improvement in mood and general quality of life
How much weight will I lose?
The amount of weight someone loses after weight loss surgery varies from person to person.
The majority of weight loss after surgery happens within the first 6 months to 1 year. Often weight loss can be slower over the second year. On average, people can lose:
50-60% excess body weight with a gastric sleeve
60-70% excess body weight with a bypass
Excess weight means the extra weight that someone is carrying above their healthy BMI.
How much weight you lose completely depends on the changes you make to your diet, activity levels and behaviour. Some people can lose more weight. Others may lose less.
It’s not guaranteed that having weight loss surgery will reduce your weight or BMI to within the healthy range. The amount of weight you’re predicted to lose will be calculated using your weight or BMI before your operation.
What will my diet look like after weight loss surgery?
After your operation you’ll be on a modified textured diet. This means the texture of your food will be different than normal for a few weeks to allow your stomach to heal after the surgery.
It can take 6-8 weeks to return to eating solid foods. Individual advice should be provided by a specialist dietitian.
Key diet and eating behaviours after surgery
As your stomach is a new shape and size you’ll need to change the way you eat. Mindful eating means paying attention to your food when you’re eating and listening to your body’s fullness signals. After surgery you can do this by:
eating slowly
putting your fork down between bites
leaving a piece of food on your plate
getting into a routine like sitting at a table for meals
focussing on your food and doing nothing else when eating
You can also follow the 20/20/20 technique. This involves:
taking a mouthful of food about the size of a 20p
chewing this mouthful 20 times
waiting 20 seconds before having another mouthful
Regular eating
As your portion sizes will be much smaller you may need to eat 3-5 meals or planned high protein snacks per day. Your appetite and hunger will be affected after surgery. It can be tempting to miss a meal if you do not feel like eating. But it’s unlikely that you’ll be getting enough protein or nutrition if you’re not eating regular meals.
The surgery helps you to feel fuller on smaller portion sizes but if you do not eat regular meals the surgery will be limited in how it can work.
It’s recommended that you plan your meals daily and appropriate snacks, if these are required. You should try to avoid grazing (eating small amounts as and when you feel like it) throughout the day.
Regular eating after surgery can help your body get into a healthy routine. This is more likely to keep your weight off longer term.
You should also limit mealtimes to no more than 30 minutes. Avoid being tempted to reheat meals later on if you have not managed to finish them at a mealtime.
Food choices
After the operation, the focus is on foods that contain protein to prevent muscle loss as you lose weight. Examples of these foods include:
lean meats and poultry ( like beef, pork and chicken)
eggs
fish
dairy sources (like milk, cheese and yoghurt)
plant based sources (beans, pulses and lentils)
You should also consider choosing low-fat and low-sugar options to limit the calories and help you lose weight.
Fluids
It’s strongly recommended that you avoid any fizzy drinks.
These can cause pain and discomfort, they may also affect your long-term weight loss outcome. You should also think about the calories in alcohol and the effect this can sometimes have on our food choices.
You should also take small sips and avoid gulping drinks. It’s recommended that you do not eat and drink together at the same time. Wait 30 minutes before and after a meal to have a drink.
Fluids should be low calorie. Try to avoid the following that can be high in fat, sugar and calories:
full fat milk
milkshakes
standard squash
fresh fruit juices
smoothies
energy drinks
rich coffees
Will I need to take vitamins forever?
It’s essential you take additional vitamin and mineral supplements. This is because your diet after surgery will not provide enough nutrition. This is a life-long requirement.
You’ll need:
Complete A-Z Multivitamin and Mineral
Calcium and Vitamin D
Iron (Ferrous Fumarate)
Vitamin B12 injections every 3 months
Complications of weight loss surgery
As you’ll need a general anaesthetic there are potential risks including:
blood clots in legs (
deep vein thrombosis
)
blood clots in lungs (pulmonary emboli)
Some specific risks associated with a sleeve gastrectomy and gastric bypass are:
staple line bleed
staple link leak
you may develop acid reflux
internal hernia (bypass only)
wound site infection
After a gastric bypass you may be at risk of having dumping syndrome if you do not follow the dietary advice. Dumping syndrome can occur if you eat or drink something that is high in sugar or fat. This moves too quickly from the stomach to the small intestine and can cause people to feel unwell. Symptoms of this are:
tiredness
dizziness
feeling faint or sweaty (
hypoglycaemia
)
stomach cramps
You should be assessed by a qualified bariatric surgeon before your operation. You should be given the opportunity to discuss all of the risks and benefits of having surgery.
Pregnancy after weight loss surgery
It’s recommended that you should not become pregnant until at least 12-18 months after surgery. This allows time for weight loss to become stable. It’s also more likely that the you’ll be able to eat a varied nutritious diet.
Losing weight can increase fertility in some women. You should think about if you need to use contraception. You should talk to your healthcare practitioner if this is appropriate.
Gastric bypass surgery can affect how you absorb some medications. This includes the
oral contraceptive pill
. It may not be absorbed properly. You should think about using a different method of contraception like:
contraceptive implant
intrauterine device
(coil)
If you become pregnant after having weight loss surgery it’s recommended that you have:
increased nutritional blood monitoring
growth scans more often during pregnancy
You should have an appointment with the antenatal service led by a consultant. They may refer you to a specialist dietitian if appropriate.
Having surgery outside the NHS
NHS Scotland does not recommend choosing to pay to travel abroad for surgery as part of a packaged holiday. This is sometimes called surgical or bariatric tourism.
Surgical options in Scotland can appear more expensive. But you should think about the potential savings against the potential risks of travelling for surgery.
Read more about having surgery abroad
What happens if I develop excess or loose skin following surgery?
Some patients can develop loose skin following weight loss surgery. There’s no direct access to plastic surgery in NHS for people who have had weight loss surgery and it’s rarely carried out.

NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde
